1:
The witnesses meet Bildad's third and final speech less as an argument than as a retreat, and they read its very brevity as a confession. The reformed John Gill judges that Bildad answers not to disprove what Job had just urged, that the grossest offenders often go unpunished and die in peace, but rather, whether convinced of its truth or thinking Job too obstinate to be moved, tries only to possess his mind with the greatness and majesty of God, in order to deter him from applying to God in a judicial way and expecting redress from him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the opening word the same way: Bildad answers not to what Job spake last, but to what seemed most reprovable in all his discourses, his censure of God's proceedings and his desire of disputing the matter with God himself.

Over the reason for the speech's shortness the voices divide. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry commends Bildad for speaking no more on the point at issue, as one who contended for truth and not for victory, and who, whether he now began to think Job in the right or simply knew when he had said enough, would not wrangle endlessly for the last word; and Wesley agrees that Bildad and the rest now perceived that Job and they did not differ so much as they had thought, since the friends owned that the wicked might prosper for a while and Job owned they would be destroyed at the last. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hear something less generous in the silence: this is the last attack on Job, and Bildad, having little to say and that little not to the point, practically owns himself and his companions worsted in argument, attempting no formal reply but merely reiterating truisms independent of the matter in hand.

Ellicott traces the ground Bildad falls back on, the position twice assumed by Eliphaz in ch. 4:17-21 and ch. 15:14-16, and once even allowed by Job himself in ch. 14:4, the impossibility of man being just with God, so that Bildad implies the impiety of Job in maintaining his righteousness. Clarke maps the little speech in advance: God's dominion is supreme, his armies innumerable, his providence over all in vv.1-3; man cannot be justified, nor the very heavens be pure, much less man, in vv.4-6. The witnesses gather to one sense: the friends' cause has run out of words, and Bildad ends it not by refuting Job but by seeking to overawe him.
2:
With the first line of his argument Bildad exalts the sovereignty of God, and the witnesses spread out its terms. The reformed John Gill fixes the subject against a misreading: the dominion and fear are not, as Sephorno would have it, faculties in man, but belong to God, whose kingdom rules over all, over angels good and bad, over all men and nations, kings and princes, of every age and condition, a dominion absolute and uncontrollable, exercised according to his own will, accountable to none, and everlasting; and the fear joined to it is not a fear with which God himself is afraid, for he dreads none, but the terror that makes him dreadful to his creatures. The wesleyan-arminian voices press that dread home. Adam Clarke calls God an absolute sovereign whose fear is upon all the hosts of heaven, and by whose sovereignty order is established and preserved throughout the eternal world, so that he has Bildad ask how Job could dare to appeal to him. John Wesley reads dominion as sovereign power over all persons and things, and fear as the terror that justly makes God dreadful to all men, and especially to those who undertake to dispute with him.

On the second clause, that he "maketh peace in his high places," the witnesses turn to the harmony of the upper world. Wesley pictures God keeping and ruling all persons in heaven in peace and concord: the angels, numberless as they are, all own his sovereignty and acquiesce in his pleasure, and the stars, vast in bulk and various in motion, keep exactly the order he has appointed, so that it is great folly for Job to quarrel with God's dealings. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gathers the whole into a sentence: God is absolute in sovereignty and terrible in power, so that even in his high places, and among his celestial hosts, he maintaineth peace and harmony.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, both weigh the words and measure the speech. They pass on the Latin verdict of Schultens over this last trumpet-blast from the friends' side, that it sounds more like a signal for retreat than for the renewing of battle, and reduce Bildad's whole speech to two commonplaces: that man cannot maintain his supposedly perverted right before God the all-just and all-controlling One, to whom even the things of heaven cheerfully submit, and that man cannot be accounted spotlessly pure before the most holy One. On the grammar they note that the word rendered "dominion" is an infinitive absolute pressed into service as a noun, and that the causative form here, without losing its force, signifies simply to exercise authority, to rule. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the peace of God's high places is the very sovereignty before which a mortal's contention must fall silent.
3:
The rhetorical question, "Is there any number of his armies?", sends the witnesses to count what cannot be counted. The reformed John Gill spreads the muster wide. There are God's armies in heaven, the innumerable host of angels, more than twelve legions, thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand, employed in a military way for the safety of the saints; there are the sun, moon, and stars, the host of heaven whose stars cannot be numbered and which fought in their courses against Sisera; and there are his armies on earth, all the inhabitants of it, yea every creature down to the smallest insect, so that even frogs and lice and flies and locusts served as the armies of God with which he fought against Pharaoh and the Egyptians. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps the same reckoning briefly, the angels, the stars, and the other creatures all his hosts, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the moral of their number: God has troops innumerable and can serve himself of all his creatures, so that everything may be a means of help or of destruction; when he purposes to save, none can destroy, and when he is determined to destroy, none can save, and it is vain to trust in his creatures against himself.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott turns the armies toward the argument Bildad is building. God is so glorious that he dispenses of his glory to his innumerable hosts of angels; glorious as they are, they do but reflect his glory, and what then must that glory itself be? If even the shining ones are but borrowers of his light, how utterly hopeless for man to think he can have any purity to compete with God's, man who is by nature and birth unclean, as the psalmist owns in Ps. 51:5.

On the closing clause, "upon whom doth not his light arise," the witnesses read the sweep of providence. Clarke takes it of God's universal lordship: he causes his sun to arise on the evil and the good, and sends his rain on the just and the unjust. Wesley hears in the light communicated to every part of the world a faint resemblance of the cognisance and care God takes of the whole creation, for all are under the light of his knowledge, all partake of the light of his goodness, his pleasure is to show mercy, and all the creatures live upon his bounty. The witnesses do not divide; they let the two images work as one, the numberless armies and the all-reaching light, to press upon Job the sheer immensity of the God he had asked to reason with, before whom the very hosts of heaven are a borrowed brightness and a marshalled obedience.
4:
Now Bildad drives at his conclusion, that no man can be justified or clean before God, and the witnesses both expound the question and quarrel with the use he makes of it. The reformed John Gill grants the truth of the words while denying their force against Job: since God sees all a man's ways and works, his secret as well as his open sins, no man can be more just than God, nor just as God is, nor be justified in his sight by a righteousness of his own, for the best righteousness of man is imperfect. Yet if Bildad took this to be the very thing Job had denied, Gill says, he mistook him; for what Job meant by coming to the seat of God and ordering his cause before him, not doubting he should be acquitted, was the justification of his cause and not of his person, that he might be cleared of the imputation of hypocrisy, and not that he might be reckoned sinless.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns that the question is no true conclusion from Bildad's premises, yet is of the highest importance to man, and one that neither Bildad nor any of his fellows could answer, since the doctrine of redemption through the blood of the cross was then known only through types and shadows. With what shall miserable man be justified with God? By bringing forward, by faith, the sacrificial offering of the Lord Jesus Christ, and confiding in it as a full atonement; and how shall he be clean that is born of a woman? By receiving that grace which applies to the heart the efficacy of the blood that cleanses from all unrighteousness. This, Clarke says, is the only way a penitent sinner can be justified and a believer sanctified, and without it there can be no glorification.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the very word for "man": it signifies the man that is miserable, which supposes him sinful; and shall such a creature quarrel with that dominion of God to which the sinless and glorious angels submit, or think to stand justified before the tribunal to which he has so boldly appealed? The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, giving the plain rendering of the lines, set the verse where Bildad means it, at the head of the descent that will run from the mortal born of woman down through the moon and stars to the worm. The witnesses do not finally divide over the doctrine, for all confess that man cannot stand justified in himself before God; but Gill and Clarke alike observe that Bildad wields a great truth clumsily, hurling at Job a maxim he had never contested, and offering no answer at all to the deeper question of how a guilty man might, after all, be made clean.
5:
The image of the dimmed heavens gives the witnesses both a picture and a puzzle: in what sense are the moon and stars "not pure" in God's sight? The reformed John Gill reads the impurity as wholly relative: survey all that is glorious in the world below, or all from the seat of the Divine Majesty down to that bright luminary the moon, and it loses its lustre and brightness the moment it is compared with the Divine Being. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, expounding the same figure, agrees that the lights of heaven shine not and are not pure, not by any defect of their own but by reason of the glory which excelleth, as a candle, though it burn, gives no shine when it is set in the clear light of the sun; the glory of God eclipses the brightest creatures, as in the day when the moon shall be confounded and the sun ashamed of Isa. 24:23. Yet Henry adds a second thought that leans the other way, that God sees spots in the moon and stars which we never see, and could as easily discover in Job what Job was not himself aware of.

That second note is where the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke plants his whole reading, for he finds the impurity intrinsic. The moon shineth not because it is continually changing, never showing the same face twice, ever waxing or waning, variegated with opaque spots; its changeableness can never be compared with the unchangeable nature of God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the heavens the same way: pure and chaste as their light is, the stars are not clean before him, for they rise and set, and once in every month the moon hides her face. So a real difference runs under the verse, whether the heavens are impure only by comparison, outshone by a greater glory, as Gill and Henry chiefly hold, or impure in themselves, spotted and inconstant, as Clarke and Ellicott urge.

Clarke alone raises, and then declines, a further reading. Some think that by "stars" are meant the angels who kept not their first estate; that may be so, he allows, but he cannot see it in the text, and hesitates over such applications. He suspects the speech was delivered in the night season, when clouds interrupted the moon's shining, and that the sun goes unmentioned because it was then below the horizon; and he does not spare Bildad's logic, calling the speech confused and inconclusive, its reasoning absurd and its conclusions falsely drawn from the premises. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley keeps to the plainer sense: the moon, bright and glorious as it is, is without lustre compared with the Divine Majesty, and in naming the moon and passing to the stars Bildad takes in the sun as well. The witnesses converge on Bildad's point even while parting over his physics: set beside God, the very lamps of heaven are dim.
6:
Bildad ends where his descent has been tending, at man the worm, and with this the witnesses close the friends' long argument. The reformed John Gill unfolds the figure: man's original is of the earth, he dwells in it, is supported by it, and creeps into it again; he is impure by nature and by practice, weak and impotent, mean and despicable. And Gill turns the comparison toward grace. If the best of men are but such creatures, and if our Lord himself in human nature was content to be called a worm and no man, as the psalm has it in Ps. 22:6, what must the worst of men be, or man in and of himself, without the grace of God and the righteousness of Christ by which alone he can be made clean? If the very lamps of heaven are eclipsed of their brightness in the presence of God, what a contemptible figure must man make in the court of heaven, who beside them is but a worm.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke works the Hebrew hard. The verse is degradingly expressive: the word for man, enosh, is the miserable man, and the word rendered "worm," rimmah, is a crawling worm; while "the son of man" is toleah, a worm or rather a maggot, so named, on Parkhurst's account, from its eating into and dividing certain substances. Almost all the versions, Clarke notes, read "Truly man is corruption, and the son of man a worm," and the Targum turns the parallel to "How much more man, who in his life is a reptile, and the son of man, who in his death is a worm," so that the two clauses may be read to divide man's meanness between his living and his dying. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott simply sets the verse beside its kindred, the "what is man" of Ps. 8:4, the worm of Ps. 22:6, and the "thou worm Jacob" of Isa. 41:14.

With this word the friends fall silent for good, and Clarke marks the ending. Thus endeth Bildad the Shuhite, who endeavoured to speak on a subject he did not understand, and, having got upon bad ground, was soon confounded in his own mind, spoke incoherently, argued inconclusively, and came abruptly and suddenly to an end; and so, his three friends being confounded, Job was left to pursue his own way, and they trouble him no more. The witnesses do not divide. They read the worm as the last and lowest rung of Bildad's ladder from the sovereign God down to fallen man, a truth truly told and yet, in his mouth, turned to no comfort, the friends' final word being not an answer to Job but a confession that they have none.
